Hollywood Cemetary borders Randolph on the southeast. A hilly area containing very many mature oaks, maples, and holly, it extends from Idlewood Avenue to the James River. The cemetery is of historical interest being the final resting place of John Tyler, James Monroe, and Jefferson Davis, as well as thousands of Civil War soldiers including Generals Jeb Stuart and George Pickett.
Riverview Cemetery and the Maymount Community border Randolph on the south separated by Colorado Avenue. Riverview Cemetery is expected to actively function for twenty or more years. Similar in topography and character of Hollywood Cemetery, it is well maintained.
The Maymont Community to the west and south is a black community of approximately 2,000 members residing in single family detached homes that reflect the care and maintenance they are given. Little if any blight or blighting influences are evident. This community is represented by the Maymont Civic League and they have often met with the Randolph Planing Study Board to negotiate and plan areas of mutual interest. A good working relationship is enjoyed by both groups.
Byrd Park and Davis Avenue adjacent to Byrd Park constitute the western border of Randolph. Byrd Park is Richmond's largest park and its offers a wide range of recreational activities, active and passive, and receives heavy use by city and county residents. It is a focal point for the city and is used for tennis matches as well as family picnics. Byrd Park along with the three cemeteries (Hollywood, Riverview, and Mount Cavalry) ring Randolph in visual and partially usuable open space.
C. Purpose of the Project
1. The purpose of the Randolph Project is to assist the City of Richmond as outlined in Title I of the Housing Act of 1949, as amended, to provide the opportunity for new housing and elimination and the prevention of further blight through rehabilitation and redevelopment. Most of the project area reflects at least two of the following deficiencies. 
a. Overcrowding or improper location of structures on the land.
b. Excessive dwelling unit density.
c. Conversions to incompatible use or use relationships.
